claims.text: Chemical short-range ordering at grain boundaries lowers grain-boundary mobility at high temperatures.
Reduced grain-boundary mobility slows grain coarsening.
Slower grain coarsening stabilizes a single-phase structure during thermal exposure.
A W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf refractory high-entropy nanoalloy can retain nanocrystallinity with limited grain coarsening under energetic high-temperature irradiation conditions.
The proposed initial W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy is a nominally single-phase solid solution.
The proposed initial alloy has limited initial short-range order.
Controlled pre-annealing schedules can produce otherwise comparable samples with different degrees of short-range order.
High-entropy and refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit chemical short-range ordering at elevated temperatures.
Short-range order locally reduces grain-boundary energy.
Slower grain-boundary migration limits compositional segregation during thermal exposure.
Samples with greater pre-induced short-range order will exhibit slower grain growth than SRO-minimized baseline samples.
Samples with greater pre-induced short-range order will retain more uniform grain-boundary compositions than SRO-minimized baseline samples.
The influence of short-range order on defect mobility becomes weaker as temperature increases.
The proposed stabilization vanishes above a critical temperature at which short-range order is destroyed.
Materials not prone to short-range ordering will show no SRO-dependent difference in grain-boundary mobility.
Secondary-phase precipitation, irradiation defects, or solute clustering could mask the contribution of short-range order.
Equal grain-coarsening and segregation rates in high-SRO and SRO-minimized samples under identical conditions would falsify a significant SRO stabilization effect.
